All six signals are now NeuroKit2-based (this replaces an earlier version of this report where LF/HF/VLF used a hand-rolled scipy.signal.welch call instead — corrected). SD2 and VLF use a 5-minute window (not 60s) because both need a longer, stationary span to be meaningful — SD2 per the project's own windowing convention, VLF because its lower frequency edge (0.0033 Hz) has a ~300s period, so anything shorter can't resolve it at all. Same 10s step for every signal so all six line up on one shared time axis.

Metric Definitions & Literature Associations

MetricDefinitionTypical association (literature)
RMSSDRoot mean square of successive R-R interval differences.Primary time-domain marker of vagally-mediated (parasympathetic) HRV; closely tracks HF power.
HRBeats per minute.Cycle-length dependent — faster HR mechanically reduces HRV. Resting HR >90bpm linked to elevated mortality risk.
SD2Poincaré plot: SD of points along the line-of-identity (long-term variability).Reflects short- and long-term HRV together; correlates with LF power and baroreflex sensitivity.
LFPower in 0.04–0.15 Hz band (≥2 min recording).Reflects baroreflex activity, not cardiac sympathetic tone specifically — mixed parasympathetic/sympathetic/BP-regulation origin.
HFPower in 0.15–0.40 Hz band (≥1 min recording).Reflects parasympathetic activity, tracks the respiratory cycle. Lower HF associated with stress/anxiety/worry.
VLFPower in 0.0033–0.04 Hz band (≥5 min, ideally 24h recording).More strongly associated with all-cause mortality than LF or HF. Low VLF linked to arrhythmic death and PTSD.
DFA α1Detrended fluctuation analysis slope, short-term scales.Short-term correlations in RR intervals reflect baroreceptor reflex function.

Source (only source used for this table): Shaffer F, Ginsberg JP (2017). An Overview of Heart Rate Variability Metrics and Norms. Frontiers in Public Health, 5:258.

Visual read per person

Written by looking directly at each person's chart, not from any shape-detection code — the point was to describe what the shape actually looks like against the expected Stage 4 (activation) / Stage 10 (rebound) map, not to algorithmically score it.

ParticipantVisual read (by inspection, no algorithmic peak-detection)
P2Flat/quiet through S1-S7 (all signals near baseline). No Stage-4 dip. A dramatic late surge instead — SD2/LF/HF/VLF all spike from S8 onward, peaking around S9-S10.
P3HR declines steadily from the start and stays low throughout. Other signals flat through S1-S6, then increasingly noisy and elevated from ~S7 onward, peaking near the very end of the session.
P4RMSSD/SD2 dip and stay suppressed through most of the middle session; deepest trough right at S9; partial rise into S10-12. (Stage-4-specific claim checked earlier and did not hold — S4 is a small bump, not a dip.)
P5Noisy throughout. RMSSD actually rises (not dips) at S4. Broad RMSSD/HF/VLF elevation around S10, loosely consistent with the expected rebound.
P6Modest dip near S4, a first rise at S5-6, then a second, bigger rise at S9-11. One of the better matches to a two-phase activation/recovery shape.
P7Flat until a dramatic, sharp single spike right at S9 across RMSSD/SD2/LF/HF/VLF together, with HR mirroring it as a sharp dip. The cleanest, most dramatic single-event response in the cohort — landing one stage after the theoretical S10 peak.
P8Noisy early (S1-4), then flat and suppressed from S5 all the way through S12 — no in-session dip, no in-session rebound. A sharp release only appears after the session ends.
P9VLF rises and peaks around S6-9, then declines through S10-12 — activation arrives early and fades exactly where the theory expects a peak.
P10RMSSD jumps up early (~S2) and stays elevated for the entire rest of the session — an early, sustained calm plateau. No Stage-4 dip, no distinct late rebound.
P11Quiet through S1-4, then a sustained noisier/elevated state from S5 onward, with a notable HF spike right at S10.
P12The cleanest match to the textbook shape: SD2 shows a genuine dip right at S4, then a sustained rise through S9-S10.

Section 3 · Aggregated Stats: Recovery % and SD2 Arc

Recovery % — percent change in a metric from the pre-session resting baseline to the post-session resting baseline: 100 × (post − pre) / pre. Positive means the metric was higher after the session than before.
SD2 arc (redefined) — the difference between the highest and lowest SD2 seen during the session itself (highest − lowest, in ms). Pre/post baseline periods are excluded from this specific search, since a participant may have moved or adjusted position during rest, which would contaminate the search for the session's own real high/low. This replaces the earlier fixed Stage 10 − Stage 4 definition, which assumed the peak and trough always land on those exact two stages — not something we've been able to confirm holds across people.

Median across 11 participants: RMSSD recovery +8.7%, SD2 recovery +3.2%, DFA α1 recovery -1.1%, HR recovery -2.5%, SD2 arc 42.6ms (session high 75.1 − low 24.9). Median used instead of mean because Ouida's +515% RMSSD recovery would otherwise dominate a mean (see note below).

Ouida's outlier RMSSD recovery (+515%) is real, not a data error — pre=9.2ms, post=57.5ms, a genuine 6x change; expressing any change relative to a very low starting value produces a large percentage by construction. Kept as-is, flagged here rather than filtered (see prior discussion — no physiological-limits rule would catch it, since neither raw value is implausible).

Recovery %, per participant

Recovery % = 100 × (post − pre) / pre. DFA α1 dropped (too complicated to interpret directly here; see it in the Section 1 signals chart instead). HR sign reversed — a drop in HR is the good/recovered direction, so it now shows as a positive bar, consistent with RMSSD/SD2.

Section 4 · Participant × Acoustic Feature Coupling

One heatmap per metric (HR/RMSSD/SD2 no longer mixed into one cell). Each cell = best |r| for that (participant, feature) pair, lag up to 30s, feature leads. Rows and columns are hierarchically clustered (average linkage) so similar participants/features sit next to each other instead of alphabetical order — the trees (dendrograms) show that grouping: two items joining low are very similar, joining high up means they're quite different despite still ending up in the same tree. This is descriptive (finds structure already in the numbers), not a new statistical test.
